e38a2c73b8eb: The Big Book says no, from its members' experience: "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). "We are like men who have lost their legs; they never grow new ones." (p. 30).

(p. 30). Many pursue it "into the gates of insanity or death" (p. 30). - "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). Periods when members thought they were regaining control were "inevitably followed by still less control" (p. 30). - "We are like men who have lost their legs; they never grow new ones." (p. 30). There doesn't appear to be any treatment that will make alcoholics of their kind "like other men" (pp. 30–31). - "Physicians who are familiar with alcoholism agree there is no such thing as making a normal drinker out of an alcoholic." (p. 31). - If anyone showing inability to control his drinking can turn around and "drink like a gentleman, our hats are off to him" (p. 31). The book isn't forbidding anyone to try; it is reporting that its members tried "hard enough and long enough" (p. 31) and couldn't. - The man of thirty who stayed bone dry until he retired at fifty-five, then believed his long sobriety had qualified him "to drink as other men": in two months he was in hospital, and he was dead within four years (pp. 32–33). e8d2a21d6ed1: Each time it points to action that follows: working with other alcoholics (p. 14), making amends (p. 76), and the Twelfth Step (p. 88).

981d4a8f8f68: <0>"Bill's Story," p. 14.</0> Bill's friend, who brought him the message, stressed working with others as he had worked with Bill. "Faith without works was dead, he said" (p. 14). Bill adds that this was "appallingly true for the alcoholic" and explains why: an alcoholic who doesn't work for others won't survive the hard times, and "If he did not work, he would surely drink again, and if he drank, he would surely die" (p. 15).
a9547dbec50a: <0>Chapter 6, p. 76.</0> Right after the Seventh Step prayer: "Now we need more action, without which we find that 'Faith without works is dead'" (p. 76). The next lines start Steps Eight and Nine, making amends.

bd20cd6eb4f8: It's often cited only to page 88. The text shows the phrase on pages 14 and 76 as well.

3e210a554c1a: Chapter 7 says the same thing in other words when it describes a newcomer who already has religious faith. He may show "that faith alone is insufficient. To be vital, faith must be accompanied by self sacrifice and unselfish, constructive action" (p. 93). Bill's story closes on the same note: faith has to work in and through us all day, every day, or we perish (p. 16).

The Big Book doesn't name a source: the only James mentioned in the main text or the appendices is the psychologist William James (pp. 28, 567). bf7e553f4d67: Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward" (pp. 122–135), says stopping drinking is only a beginning: "Cessation of drinking is but the first step away from a highly strained, abnormal condition." (p. 122). A doctor told the members that years of living with an alcoholic make the whole family, to some extent, ill (p. 122).
d70bcac90ef8: Its answer is that every member of the family, the alcoholic included, should "meet upon the common ground of tolerance, understanding and love" (p. 122), which means each one giving up the demand to have things his or her way.
feed8c6cf0a6: It names the usual troubles: expecting the good old days back at once, digging up the past, the man who rushes to rebuild his finances or who becomes a religious enthusiast, the shift of authority at home, jealousy of his new activities, and children slow to forgive.
3fa3e5d1e86b: It closes on health and happiness: see good doctors, don't belittle them (p. 133), and enjoy life: "We absolutely insist on enjoying life." (p. 132).
80285c45fa24: The chapter begins by correcting an impression Chapter 8 might give, that the recovering husband is to be wrapped in cotton wool and put on a pedestal: "Successful readjustment means the opposite." (p. 122). Each person in the family has fixed ideas about how the others should treat him or her, and "the more one member of the family demands that the others concede to him, the more resentful they become" (p. 122). The question it asks of everyone: "Is he not unconsciously trying to see what he can take from the family life rather than give?" (p. 122).
00e43055b1a8: <0>Wanting it all back now.</0> The family remembers father as he once was and expects the good old days back at once. But the wreckage of years "will take time to clear away" (p. 123); the new structures "will take years to complete" (p. 123). "The wise family will admire him for what he is trying to be, rather than for what he is trying to get." (p. 123).
7842e1b80a0f: <0>The past.</0> The first impulse is to lock the skeletons in a closet. The chapter calls that self-centered: the alcoholic's past "thus becomes the principal asset of the family" (p. 124), because it can help other families still struggling. But dragging up old misdeeds in anger, such as a past affair, can become "a veritable plague" (p. 124); unless some good purpose is served, "past occurrences should not be discussed" (p. 125). And "we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve" (p. 125).
2dc0c8fb07e5: <0>The man who rushes at money.</0> If he throws himself into rebuilding his finances, the family feels neglected and resentful; he feels unappreciated (pp. 125–126). Both are partly right. The family should remember "dad, though marvelously improved, is still convalescing" (p. 127). He should remember he is "mainly to blame for what befell his home" (p. 127). "For us, material well-being always followed spiritual progress; it never preceded." (p. 127).
c23979d338fd: <0>The man who becomes a religious enthusiast.</0> If instead he has a stirring spiritual experience and talks of nothing else, the family may resent "a God who has stolen dad's affections" (p. 128). The chapter's advice: let him have his head, even let him go as far as he likes in helping other alcoholics in the first days; it will do more for his sobriety than anything else (p. 129), and he'll come down to earth sooner in an understanding family (p. 129). e8ecc3da607b: The Foreword to the First Edition is under two pages long (pp. xiii–xiv). The fourth edition prints it "as it appeared in the first printing of the first edition in 1939" (p. xiii). Read straight through, it says six things.
0c0161530eb2: <0>Who "we" are.</0> More than a hundred men and women who have recovered from "a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii).
b2e3b2acfc9c: <0>What the book is for.</0> "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered is the main purpose of this book." (p. xiii). The hope is that the account will convince them without further proof, help everyone understand that the alcoholic "is a very sick person" (p. xiii), and show that this way of living has advantages for all (p. xiii).
3df6a92c5403: <0>Why the members are anonymous.</0> The reason it gives is practical: there were too few of them to handle all the personal appeals the book might bring, and most had jobs to keep: "We would like it understood that our alcoholic work is an avocation." (p. xiii). Members writing or speaking in public are asked to call themselves "a member of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. xiii), and the press is asked to respect that (p. xiii).
6cdb68c59d56: <0>What A.A. is not.</0> It is not an organization in the conventional sense of the word (pp. xiii–xiv). "There are no fees or dues whatsoever." (p. xiv).
a134f4807fd9: <0>Who can belong.</0> "The only requirement for membership is an honest desire to stop drinking." (p. xiv). A.A. is not allied with any faith, sect or denomination, and opposes no one (p. xiv).
6c103920deea: <0>What it wants.</0> "We simply wish to be helpful to those who are afflicted." (p. xiv). It asks to hear from readers who are getting results, "particularly from those who have commenced work with other alcoholics" (p. xiv), and offers to help them. It welcomes inquiry from scientific, medical and religious societies (p. xiv).
b0e8502051ac: In 1939 the fellowship's stated purpose was to help alcoholics recover, and the book was the way to reach the ones the members couldn't reach in person. The foreword's one request of its readers is about carrying the message: it wants to hear most from those who have started working with other alcoholics, the work Chapter 7 describes (see <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>).
246de6c9fef9: Nothing in the foreword sets up rules for members, a program of meetings, or any kind of authority. It describes a loose fellowship of people helping drinkers.
e702641c0f55: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) quotes the foreword's sentences about fees, membership and faith and says that, "With a few changes and additions," that statement of purpose came to be read as a preamble at meetings (Pass It On, 1984). 73db821838d0: What does "deep down in every man, woman, and child is the fundamental idea of God" say?
e2fcb8490aa1: The line is on page 55 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics": "deep down in every man, woman, and child, is the fundamental idea of God" (p. 55). It goes on: the idea may be hidden "by calamity, by pomp, by worship of other things, but in some form or other it is there" (p. 55).
68d8ce7781d8: It is a claim about everyone, and the context doesn't soften the wording. What the context adds is how it's offered: as former agnostics admitting something about themselves ("Actually we were fooling ourselves," p. 55), with "in some form or other," and closing on "It was so with us." (p. 55)
0cf815180852: The next lines say where they found God: "We found the Great Reality deep down within us." (p. 55) "In the last analysis it is only there that He may be found." (p. 55) Then they limit their own part: "We can only clear the ground a bit." (p. 55)
62cc26e88683: So context complicates any use of the line, quoted alone, as a ruling on what other people secretly believe. In its place it's testimony, and it sends the reader to search within himself rather than to take the writers' word for it.
a46996a7e703: The chapter has been arguing that reason isn't everything (p. 54). The people who proved man could never fly were reasoning too (p. 55). Then the writers turn the flying image around: they had been seeing "another kind of flight, a spiritual liberation from this world, people who rose above their problems" (p. 55). "They said God made these things possible, and we only smiled." (p. 55) "We had seen spiritual release, but liked to tell ourselves it wasn't true." (p. 55)
e0677165e896: That's the setup. The line itself opens with a confession: "Actually we were fooling ourselves, for deep down..." (p. 55). The writers are telling the reader what they found out about themselves.
d956402e9f38: In order (p. 55): 1. The fundamental idea of God is deep down in everyone, though calamity, pomp or the worship of other things may hide it. 2. Faith in a Power greater than ourselves, and its "miraculous demonstrations" in human lives, "are facts as old as man himself" (p. 55). 3. "We finally saw that faith in some kind of God was a part of our make-up, just as much as the feeling we have for a friend." (p. 55) 4. "Sometimes we had to search fearlessly, but He was there." (p. 55) 5. "We found the Great Reality deep down within us." (p. 55) "In the last analysis it is only there that He may be found." (p. 55) "It was so with us." (p. 55) 6. "We can only clear the ground a bit." (p. 55) If their testimony helps the reader drop prejudice and think honestly, and "encourages you to search diligently within yourself" (p. 55), then "if you wish" (p. 55), the reader can join them on the Broad Highway.
ddedab6f869c: Notice the wording that keeps it open: "in some form or other," "some kind of God," "if you wish." And notice where the passage points: inward. It doesn't send the reader to a church, a creed or the writers' own beliefs, but "deep down within us" (p. 55).
a619f31c25ca: The chapter closes with the man who thought he was an atheist. Alone in a hospital room, he asked himself whether all the religious people he'd known could be wrong, and then the thought came: "Who are you to say there is no God?" (p. 56) His change was sudden. The book adds that it isn't so for everyone: "Some of us grow into it more slowly." (p. 57) Appendix II, added after the first printing (p. 567), says most members' experiences are slow, and that they find they have "tapped an unsuspected inner resource" (pp. 567–568), which they come to identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves (p. 568).
e2a19f2a87ae: It complicates it. The book does claim that the idea of God is deep down in everyone, and a fair page has to say so. But in its place the claim is the writers' testimony about what they found when they stopped fooling themselves. It's held open ("in some form or other"), it points the reader to look within, and the writers say all they can do is clear the ground. The chapter's own starting requirement, a few pages earlier, is only willingness to believe (p. 47).

a7a0fa845d4a: The line is on page 53 of the Big Book, in Chapter 4, "We Agnostics," a chapter written in the voice of members who had thought they were atheists or agnostics, for readers who still are (pp. 44, 53).
7fb5710e07b7: In place, it describes the choice the writers say they faced once alcoholism had crushed them: "God either is, or He isn't. What was our choice to be?" (p. 53) The book does present it as a question that couldn't be dodged, and it argues that believing is more reasonable than leaving it at "We don't know" (p. 53).
a4ebde408e14: The same chapter says how small the start can be. Willingness to believe in a Power greater than yourself is enough to begin (pp. 46–47), and "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). The either-or is about whether God is, not about which idea of God to accept.
c65a724b4a67: So context complicates the reading of the line as an ultimatum. The choice is real and stark in the book. But it's the writers' account of their own turning point, argued for at length, inside a chapter that asks only for willingness at the start.
0f9ce43fe00f: Page 53 begins by praising reason: "Logic is great stuff. We liked it. We still like it." (p. 53) The power to reason is "one of man's magnificent attributes" (p. 53). The writers, being "agnostically inclined," wouldn't be satisfied with a proposal that couldn't be reasonably approached, so they set out to explain "why we think it more sane and logical to believe than not to believe" (p. 53). They call their old habit of throwing up their hands and saying they didn't know "soft and mushy" (p. 53).
9bae245070de: Then the line. When they became alcoholics, crushed by a crisis they couldn't postpone or evade, they had to face "the proposition that either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53). "Arrived at this point, we were squarely confronted with the question of faith." (p. 53)
0dc85bfec6a7: The next paragraphs describe how that felt: - <0>The bridge.</0> Some of them had "walked far over the Bridge of Reason toward the desired shore of faith" (p. 53), and were grateful reason had brought them so far, but "somehow, we couldn't quite step ashore" (p. 53). - <1>Faith all along.</1> They saw they had already been living by a kind of faith: faith in their own reasoning (pp. 53–54), and worship of people, money, themselves, or a sunset (p. 54). "Hence, we saw that reason isn't everything." (p. 54) - <2>Where they looked.</2> They came to see that faith in some kind of God was part of their make-up, and that "We found the Great Reality deep down within us." (p. 55) - <3>Stepping ashore.</3> The chapter ends with the story of a minister's son who thought he was an atheist; after the thought "Who are you to say there is no God?" (p. 56), "He had stepped from bridge to shore." (p. 56)

3649b381476a: Is group conscience a majority vote?
ea82189a2b49: The Long Form doesn't say. Tradition Two names the group conscience as the way "a loving God" expresses Himself for the group's purpose (p. 563), and it says nothing about votes, majorities or procedure.
47564a2826f8: Groups did vote from the start: the Long Form has them electing secretaries and committees (p. 565). But Bill W.'s 1946 essay on money says the majority "ought not to try to coerce" the minority (there, into paying for clubs it doesn't want), and his 1947 essays say the group's leaders only carry out what they believe the group wants.
c7a46e239916: The idea that a group conscience means "substantial unanimity," reached after everyone has been heard, is spelled out in later literature (the 1962 Concepts; the 2018 group pamphlet). Even there, the group still votes in the end.
f5bf9534c7db: So: not simply a show of hands, and not a rule against voting either. The early texts protect the minority more than they prescribe a method.
3d1b82d748a2: What the Long Form says, and doesn't
13a11f73512b: Tradition Two: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." (p. 563). That's the whole of it. The group conscience is where the Tradition locates the authority, but the text doesn't describe how a group arrives at it.
b33e72a0ee98: Other Traditions show that groups made decisions in ordinary ways. "The small group may elect its secretary, the large group its rotating committee" (p. 565). Those elected are "trusted and experienced servants of the whole" who "do not govern" (p. 565). Elections were normal; government by the winners was not.
b34bf5b8eca8: What the 1946–47 essays say about majorities
2c9c0b65d472: The earliest texts on the question come from money and clubs, the subjects that divided groups most.
8f1bbf681750: <0>The majority can't make the minority pay.</0> In "Money" (1946) Bill notes that most members like clubs, but "the majority ought not to try to coerce" (P-17, "Money", 1946) the minority into supporting clubs they don't want or need. Clubs should be paid for by the people who want them.
95f538a7b339: <0>A majority view doesn't make policy by itself.</0> In "Clubs in A.A." (1947) he writes that "Were a vote taken tomorrow on the desirability of clubs a sizable majority of A.A.s would record a resounding 'yes'" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947). He takes the "strong minority" who wanted no part of clubs just as seriously, and the answer A.A. settled on served both: "A.A.s who need and want clubs ought to have them" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947), kept separate from the groups.
35d8b4eeb5df: <0>Committees serve the group's wishes.</0> In "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?" (1947): "Each committee carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group." (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). Leaders can guide by example or persuasion but "can never boss" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947). The New York office could "usually tell how the majority of A.A.s feel about our current problems" (P-17, "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947), but that made it a source of information, not a ruler.
782de2976370: None of this says how many hands make a decision. It does say a majority isn't entitled to coerce, and that knowing what most members think is useful, not binding on everyone.
5c2af20a4007: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> Bill describes learning that the conscience of the group, "when properly informed of the facts and issues and principles involved" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957), was often wiser than any leader. The stress is on being informed: facts, issues and principles, not just a count.
da3485dba17d: The word "unanimity" comes into the literature later. Concept XII (Bill W., 1962) asks that the Conference reach all important decisions "by discussion, vote, and, whenever possible, by substantial unanimity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). P-16 (2018) quotes the same line as "wherever possible."
3d4076bc05b3: The A.A. group pamphlet (P-16, 2018) applies that to groups. It describes group conscience as representing "substantial unanimity on an issue before definitive action is taken" (P-16, 2018), with a "willingness to listen to minority opinions with an open mind" (P-16, 2018). On sensitive issues the group goes slowly, and the result "rests on more than a 'yes' or 'no' count" (P-16, 2018). But it also says all views are heard "before the group votes" (P-16, 2018), and that at business meetings "minority, or dissenting, views be heard along with those of the majority" (P-16, 2018). In this account the vote still happens. It comes last, after the listening.
b6e47a5e9aca: The text of Tradition Two doesn't settle the mechanics, and we shouldn't pretend it does. What the early writing does settle is the spirit: no one rules, the minority isn't steamrolled, and those who serve carry out the group's wishes rather than their own. A group that votes after a full hearing is consistent with all of it. A narrow majority pushing through something a large minority opposes runs against the spirit of what Bill wrote in 1946 and 1947, though his only direct words on it are about making the minority pay for clubs.

0b29e7b8a09e: Can an A.A. group be named after a treatment centre or a person?
382201366148: The 1946 Long Form doesn't mention group names. What it says is that a group may cooperate with anyone but must never go so far as "affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564), and that a group counts as an A.A. group only if, as a group, it has "no other affiliation" (p. 563).
ad09df536443: The specific naming advice comes later, from P-16 (2018): a group meeting in a treatment facility, a church or a prison should not use the institution's name, so it's clear the group only rents space there.
cd7cbc6e4e6e: P-16 also reports a General Service Conference recommendation that no group be named after any actual person, living or dead, as a way to place "principles before personalities."
b9c3ee18f365: These are recommendations from group experience. The Long Form leaves each group's own affairs to its own conscience (p. 563).
d394f205c56f: <0>A group has no other affiliation.</0> Tradition Three: any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563).
57b175d83d9f: <0>Not even an implied link.</0> Tradition Six: "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied" (p. 564). "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one" (p. 564). The same paragraph says outside facilities such as clubs and hospitals "ought not to use the A.A. name" (p. 564), and that hospitals and other places of recuperation belong "well outside A.A." (p. 564).
78445cbca871: <0>Principles before personalities.</0> Tradition Twelve: anonymity reminds A.A. "to place principles before personalities" (p. 566).
d033f121201c: <0>The group decides its own affairs.</0> Tradition Four: in its own affairs each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" (p. 563), but should consult neighbouring groups when its plans affect them, and should confer with the trustees before any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole (p. 563).
af6f77b71597: None of this mentions what a group calls itself. A name, though, is the most public thing a group has. A group named after the treatment centre it meets in looks like part of that centre, which is the "implied" affiliation the Sixth Tradition warns against.
29db4f926568: What later group experience recommends (P-16, 2018, dated)
b79a582eaf2c: The pamphlet <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16) has a section on naming (P-16, pp. 17–18):
5c070b33b458: Groups have learned to avoid any affiliation with or endorsement of any outside enterprise, "No matter how noble the activity or institution" (P-16, 2018, p. 17).
29dc230f5f22: "Even the appearance of being linked to any organization, club, or political or religious institution needs to be avoided" (P-16, 2018, p. 17).
55d3b4b48e6e: So a group meeting in a correctional or treatment facility or a church should not use the institution's name "but to call itself something quite different" (P-16, 2018, p. 18). That shows the group isn't affiliated with the place but "simply rents space there for meetings" (P-16, 2018, p. 18).
29f66a01027f: The General Service Conference has recommended that no group be named after "any actual person, living or dead, A.A. or non-A.A." (P-16, 2018, p. 18).
b64098f12675: P-16 also covers the reverse case. A treatment facility or halfway house should not carry the A.A. name, or a name like "Twelfth Step House" that wrongly implies A.A. endorsement (P-16, 2018, p. 41).
5f2180832d9d: What the text settles, and what it doesn't
79d573313bcd: The 1946 Long Form settles the principle: no affiliation, not even an implied one, and principles before personalities. It doesn't contain a naming rule. The naming guidance is later (P-16 is © 2018), and it's worded as experience and as a Conference recommendation, not a rule a group can be made to follow. No one in A.A. can force a group to change its name (see <0>Tradition Nine: is A.A. organized? Who runs it?</0>). A group choosing a name is weighing its own conscience against the Long Form's warning about implied affiliation.

8102677863c0: What is a GSR, a district and an area?
8744e52c4f3a: They are the steps between an A.A. group and the yearly General Service Conference in the U.S. and Canada. A group elects a <0>general service representative (GSR)</0>. The GSRs of nearby groups form a <1>district</1> and elect a district committee member (DCM). Districts make up an <2>area</2> (93 of them in the U.S. and Canada), whose assembly elects a <3>delegate</3> to the Conference every two years.
3958e24e407d: None of this is in the Big Book's 1939 text. It was built from 1951, when the first Conference met, and the Conference Charter (1955) set it out. Most details below come from the current <0>A.A. Service Manual</0> (2024–2026 edition) and are labelled that way.
09ab3f974606: Bill W.'s Concept IX (1962) calls GSRs, committee members and delegates "the direct agents of the A.A. groups" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). None of them governs a group.
4ababdc4a5f0: Intergroups and central offices, which the Long Form of Nine (1946) mentions, are a separate thing: local service offices, not part of this general service structure.
8e62bb43c963: The earliest text: Long Form Nine (1946)
73cae91dda27: The 1946 Long Form describes the service A.A. had then: "The small group may elect its secretary, the large group its rotating committee, and the groups of a large metropolitan area their central or intergroup committee, which often employs a full-time secretary" (p. 565). Above them were the trustees, A.A.'s General Service Committee in New York (p. 565). There were no GSRs, districts or delegates yet; the Conference that needed them came in 1951.
f61797e9b6a3: The original Conference Charter (1955) set up "State and Provincial Assemblies" of group representatives, which met every two years to elect committeemen and, from among them, a delegate "by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955). Of delegates it says: "Delegates should be free to vote as their conscience dictates" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955). In 1971 the Conference allowed states and provinces to be joined into one assembly area, and in 1978 it renamed them area assemblies, made up of GSRs, district committee members and area officers (footnotes to the Charter, Appendix K).
c79853e9f4a4: In Concept IX (1962) Bill puts the base of the whole service structure on "several thousand General Service Representatives (GSRs), several hundred area Committee Members, and nearly a hundred Delegates" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). He asks groups to choose GSRs with care: "Hit-or-miss methods should be avoided" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). Only the GSRs, meeting in assembly, name the committee members and finally the delegates.
ac86428617d0: Concept III adds what the delegate is for. Delegates are "primarily the world servants of A.A. as a whole, that only in a secondary sense do they represent their respective areas" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept III), so on final votes they should vote their own judgment and conscience.
356519044b39: How it works now (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026)
28e323c1f37f: <0>GSR.</0> Elected by a group, usually for two years, with an alternate. The manual calls the GSR "the link between the group and" A.A. as a whole and says "The GSR is that voice" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 1). A GSR attends district meetings and area assemblies with a vote, reports back to the group, and passes on the group's views. The manual suggests at least two years' sobriety. P-16, <1>The A.A. Group</1> (© 2018), calls the GSR "the group’s link with the General Service Conference" (P-16).
6c7216172da8: <0>District.</0> A cluster of groups near one another (the manual also describes language districts and, since the pandemic, virtual districts for online groups). The GSRs elect a <1>DCM</1>, who sits on the area committee. On how a DCM should lead, the manual says the GSRs will want "to be inspired and encouraged, but not told what to do" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 2).
385cce96f8c2: <0>Area.</0> "The U.S. and Canada are divided into 93 geographic areas" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Glossary), usually one per state or province, more where A.A. is large. The area assembly is made up of GSRs, DCMs, area officers and committee chairs. Every two years an election assembly chooses the delegate, usually by the Third Legacy Procedure: a two-thirds vote, or names drawn from a hat. The area also runs services too big for one group, such as public information, corrections and treatment facility work.
baba535454bf: <0>Delegate and Conference.</0> The delegate serves two years and goes to the Conference each spring in New York. It has about 135 voting members; area delegates "make up at least two-thirds of the Conference body" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Introduction), with the trustees, the directors of A.A. World Services and the Grapevine, and staff. Matters approved by two-thirds become Advisory Actions, and the delegate reports back to the area and its GSRs.
714073df5190: <0>Not bosses.</0> The current manual quotes Bill in "the first edition of this manual" (our copy gives no date; the manual grew out of his Third Legacy Manual, first drafted in 1951): "The Conference represents us, but cannot rule us" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Chapter 6). Concept XII (1962) bars the Conference from "any acts of government" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).
4c2391748742: <0>Not the intergroup.</0> Intergroups and central offices keep local meeting lists and phones. The manual says they are an important part of A.A. but "they are not part of the general service structure or a satellite of GSO" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Introduction).

3075f7520bae: It's in the past tense and about the writers themselves. The next sentences say what the whole measure was: "We stood at the turning point." (p. 59) "We asked His protection and care with complete abandon." (p. 59)
76a7b2363fbe: The paragraphs just before it name what had held them back: looking for "an easier, softer way" and holding on to "old ideas" (p. 58). "The result was nil until we let go absolutely." (p. 58)

6b3f5b191e86: The opening paragraph on who recovers and who doesn't, which turns on honesty (p. 58). See <0>What does "Rarely have we seen a person fail" really say, and who does it say may not recover?</0>
3f43501d8af1: If you want what the members have and are willing to go to any length to get it, "then you are ready to take certain steps" (p. 58).
4a9a64a9068f: "At some of these we balked." (p. 58) "We thought we could find an easier, softer way." (p. 58) "But we could not." (p. 58) The book begs the reader "to be fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58). Some had tried to hold on to their old ideas, "and the result was nil until we let go absolutely" (p. 58).
563ab101ebec: Alcohol is "cunning, baf-" (p. 58) / "fling, powerful!" (p. 59). "Without help it is too much for us." (p. 59) "But there is One who has all power—that One is God." (p. 59) "May you find Him now!" (p. 59)
b2d3ba808688: <0>"Half measures availed us nothing."</0> (p. 59) "We stood at the turning point." (p. 59) "We asked His protection and care with complete abandon." (p. 59)
786196999792: "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59).
ca0831eaab0e: The book doesn't list them. What it gives is the sentences around the line. Before it: balking at some of the steps, hunting for an easier, softer way, and holding on to old ideas, which got the same result, "nil" (p. 58). Just before it: alcohol is too much for us without help, but there is One who has all power (p. 59). After it, the whole measure: at the turning point, asking God's protection and care "with complete abandon" (p. 59).
21e7d3e1617c: So in its own place, the line sets holding back against letting go completely. "The result was nil" (p. 58) and "availed us nothing" (p. 59) are the same thought, said twice within a few lines.
2faae9dc5fe1: The sentence says "us": it reports what happened to the people who wrote the book. The paragraph around it is urgent. "With all the earnestness at our command, we beg of you to be fearless and thorough from the very start." (p. 58) But it is offered as experience, and the Steps that follow are introduced as "suggested" (p. 59). See <0>Are the Steps rules or suggestions?</0>
5ec3d4821cc9: The book separates thoroughness from perfection a page later. After the Steps, the book says many members exclaimed "What an order!" (p. 60), and it answers: "Do not be discouraged." (p. 60) "No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles." (p. 60) "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60) In its place, the line is about holding back at the turning point. It isn't about falling short of perfection afterwards.
4c08ce733439: Not much. It confirms it, and makes it clearer. The book does ask for complete commitment from the start, and says so more than once on these two pages. What context adds is what was being held back (old ideas, the search for an easier way, and trying without help), and that the line is about the turning point, not a demand to be perfect afterwards.

33b64251410d: Is HALT (hungry, angry, lonely, tired) in the Big Book?
ae704ae7754f: No. Neither the acronym HALT nor the list "hungry, angry, lonely, tired" is in the Big Book, or anywhere else in our sources.
60e0c6a60de2: Each of the four words does turn up in the program text on its own, most strongly anger: resentment "destroys more alcoholics than anything else" (p. 64). The book never puts the four together as warning signs.
6ccab39b7dd3: The book's main point about relapse cuts against any checklist of moods: Fred drank on a day when "Physically, I felt fine" and he had no worries (p. 41). The program text says that at certain times the alcoholic has no mental defense against the first drink at all, and that his defense "must come from a Higher Power" (p. 43).
07f5ca1ba8e9: All our sources were searched for "HALT," "hungry, angry" and each of the four words, and for any two of them within a sentence of each other. Nothing turned up. Where "halt" appears it is the ordinary word, as in a therapy that "came to almost a complete halt" (p. 283) or a motion that brings debate to a halt (A.A. Service Manual); one hit in <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> is a scanning error for "Half." No story in any edition in our sources uses the acronym.
0c08b1ff5947: Where the four words do appear in the program text
e76ea4fb23fa: <0>Hungry.</0> In Chapter 3, Jim's relapse begins when "On the way I felt hungry so I stopped at a roadside place where they have a bar." (p. 36). The book doesn't treat the hunger as the cause. It calls what followed, the idea that whiskey in milk on a full stomach couldn't hurt him, "plain insanity" (p. 37). Elsewhere, Chapter 9 passes on a doctor's suggestion, "of course depending upon a doctor's advice" (p. 133), to keep chocolate on hand "for its quick energy value at times of fatigue" (p. 134), since a vague craving at night could be satisfied by candy (p. 134).
70a570aef23d: <0>Angry.</0> This is the one with the most weight. Resentment is the "number one" offender, and "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (p. 64). "If we were to live, we had to be free of anger." (p. 66). A wife's nagging about her husband's smoking and coffee threw him "into a fit of anger. He got drunk." (p. 135), and the book adds that he was "dead wrong" (p. 135). Chapter 10 names "The greatest enemies of us alcoholics" as "resentment, jealousy, envy, frustration, and fear" (p. 145). Chapter 3 also says that when they drank deliberately, feeling justified "by nervousness, anger, worry, depression, jealousy or the like," the justification was "insanely insufficient in the light of what always happened" (p. 37).
21540dd28fd8: <0>Lonely.</0> Bill's own story has loneliness leading to a drink, years before A.A.: sailing for the war, "I was very lonely and again turned to alcohol." (p. 1). After that, loneliness belongs to the drinking: Bill in "that bitter morass of self-pity" (p. 8), and "the chilling vapor that is loneliness" of the last days of drinking (p. 151). In the Akron hotel lobby, Bill thought that without a few drinks he might "have a lonely week-end" (p. 154); what he did was phone a clergyman to find another alcoholic (p. 154). Chapter 7 promises the helper the chance "to watch loneliness vanish" (p. 89).
734201fd6bc0: <0>Tired.</0> Step Eleven's practice of pausing through the day ends: "We do not tire so easily, for we are not burning up energy foolishly" (p. 88). Chapter 10 warns employers that a newly sober man "may overdo" and may need his sixteen-hour days curbed (p. 146). And there is the chocolate "at times of fatigue" (p. 134).
bb084a4c7ae9: What the book puts at the centre
44c339cb06b7: Chapter 3 is the book's study of "the mental states that precede a relapse into drinking" (p. 35). Its examples don't fit a list of moods:
35560aabc036: Jim was a little irritated and hungry (p. 36), but the book's point is that "parallel with our sound reasoning there inevitably ran some insanely trivial excuse for taking the first drink" (p. 37).
5e5ffcd27bbd: Fred had no trigger at all. "Physically, I felt fine. Neither did I have any pressing problems or worries." (p. 41). It was "the end of a perfect day, not a cloud on the horizon" (p. 41), and he ordered a cocktail without thinking of the consequences (p. 41).
2c6010c628bd: The chapter's conclusion: "The alcoholic at certain times has no effective mental defense against the first drink." (p. 43), and "His defense must come from a Higher Power." (p. 43). Chapter 2 says the same: "We are without defense against the first drink." (p. 24).
8d43a42d1093: So the book does want the alcoholic watching for resentment, fear, selfishness and dishonesty, every day (pp. 84, 86), and it takes anger very seriously. But it doesn't rest safety on noticing moods or meeting physical needs. A list like HALT can be sensible advice; the Big Book's own answer to the first drink is a spiritual one, kept up daily (pp. 84–85). See: <0>Is the definition of insanity in the Big Book?</0>

(p. 132) - "We absolutely insist on enjoying life." (p. 132) The writers try not to be cynical about the state of the nations or carry the world's troubles on their shoulders (p. 132). - When they see a man sinking into alcoholism, they give him first aid and put what they have at his disposal, and for his sake they recount and almost relive the horrors of their past (p. 132). (p. 132) - Those in bad health and those who seldom play don't laugh much, so families should play, together or separately (pp. 132–133).

7374c993ac02: The next paragraph keeps its feet on the ground. "A body badly burned by alcohol does not often recover overnight nor do twisted thinking and depression vanish in a twinkling." (p. 133) The writers believe a spiritual way of living is a powerful health restorer, "But this does not mean that we disregard human health measures." f1fbd1bcdd49: When you work with a man and his family, stay out of their quarrels, help them see he has been very sick, and teach them by telling how your own home recovered, not by criticizing (p. 100).
d467b0108076: Two whole chapters are for families: Chapter 8, "To Wives," written in the voice of the wives of early members, addressed to the wives of men who drink (p. 104), and Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward."
b251256509dc: The first members did this from the start. When a man didn't recover, they tried to bring his family into a spiritual way of living (p. 159).
9b96cce28132: The family is part of the work from the first step: - <0>Before you meet him.</0> If he seems to want to stop, have a good talk with the person most interested in him, usually his wife, to learn about him (p. 90). The family should be patient, "realizing they are dealing with a sick person" (p. 90), shouldn't plead with him, and shouldn't try to tell your story (pp. 90–91). Meeting him through a doctor or hospital is better than through the family (p. 91), and leave the family out of the first talk (p. 91). - <1>If he won't respond.</1> "You should continue to be friendly to them. The family should be offered your way of life" (p. 97). If they practice spiritual principles there's a better chance he'll recover, "And even though he continues to drink, the family will find life more bearable" (p. 97). - <2>The cost.</2> Helping others may mean "counseling frantic wives and relatives" (p. 97). - <3>When he's recovering.</3> He should make what reparation he can and live his new principles at home, without fault-finding, even where the family is partly at fault (p. 98). There should be no hurry to reunite after a separation, and "Let no alcoholic say he cannot recover unless he has his family back" (p. 99). - <4>Your conduct with them.</4> "You should take care not to participate in their quarrels" (p. 100). Urge them to treat him as a very sick person, warn against resentment and jealousy, and point out his defects won't vanish overnight (p. 100). "The story of how you and your wife settled your difficulties is worth any amount of criticism" (p. 100).
7c510a7d9b8f: Written in 1939 in the voice of "the wives of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 104), for anyone "bound by ties of blood or affection to an alcoholic" (p. 104). (A note added later says it assumed the drinker was the husband because there were few women in A.A. then, p. 104.) Some of what it says: - Treat him as sick: "Treat him, when you can, as though he had pneumonia" (p. 108). It makes an exception for men who are "thoroughly bad-intentioned," and says a wife may feel she had better leave (p. 108). - "Never tell him what he must do about his drinking" (p. 111), and don't let his drinking spoil your relations with your children or friends (p. 111). - Meanwhile, "you might try to help the wife of another serious drinker" (p. 112). - Wives found they needed the program too, and urge others to try it (pp. 116–117). - When he recovers and spends long hours with other alcoholics, join him: "direct some of your thought to the wives of his new alcoholic friends" (p. 119).

c72aea694b7b: The family's painful past becomes something to give: "each family which has been relieved owes something to those who have not" (p. 124).

c33a2a1fa4db: Henrietta Seiberling was a nonalcoholic member of the Oxford Group in Akron, the daughter-in-law of the founder of the Goodyear rubber company. She lived in the gatehouse of the Seiberling estate.
4527bf91c6bb: On the Saturday before Mother's Day, May 1935, Bill W., stranded in Akron and afraid he would drink, reached her by telephone after a minister's list of names ran out. She knew of a doctor in her Oxford Group who couldn't stop drinking, and the next afternoon she brought Dr. Bob and Bill together in her home.
7f088260da42: Bill wrote that she was the only one on that list "who had understood enough and cared enough" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), and that A.A.'s debt to her was beyond reckoning. Dr. Bob called her "our good friend Henrietta."
df08f2581cca: The 1939 Big Book doesn't name her; Dr. Bob's story calls her only "a lady" (p. 179). A 1980 history, from her own and other members' recollections, shows she later disagreed with the alcoholics on money, on how much to speak of God, on the book, and on leaving the Oxford Group.
e13edd0c458a: In "Doctor Bob's Nightmare," written in 1939: "About this time a lady called up my wife one Saturday afternoon saying she wanted me to come over that evening to meet a friend of hers who might help me." (p. 179). He was in no shape that day; the next day she called again, and they went (p. 179).
